newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jury deliberates fate of Ruiz Massieu money.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jury deliberates fate of Ruiz Massieu money.

text.p: A U.S. jury on Saturday began deliberations to determine whether former Mexican deputy attorney general Mario Ruiz Massieu took millions of dollars in bribes from drug-traffickers and stashed the money in a Texas bank.
The case went to the five-man, three-woman jury after a week of testimony that focused on high-level drug corruption in Mexico and perhaps laid the groundwork for similar cases in the future.
If the jury rules that Ruiz Massieu got the money from drug-traffickers, the U.S. government will keep, pending appeal, $9 million it seized two years ago from his account in Texas Commerce Bank.

Prosecutors charged that Ruiz Massieu took bribes from Mexican drug lords in exchange for protection while he was in the Mexican Attorney General's office and supposedly a top drug-fighter in 1993 and 1994.

Witnesses included former police bodyguard Raul Macias, who said he put two suitcases full of drug cash in Ruiz Massieu's car in an August 1994 rendezvous outside the Attorney General's headquarters in downtown Mexico City.

Ruiz Massieu testified that the $9 million was part of his family's fortune, stashed in the United States for safekeeping from instability in Mexico. He said the fortune came partly from lavish government bonuses paid to high-ranking officials out of a secret budget controlled by the President of Mexico.

During the trial, U.S. prosecutors charged that drug corruption in Mexico, particularly among law enforcement officials, was rampant. "The Mexican federal judicial police, people in the PGR (Mexican Attorney General's office), deputy attorney generals or that level at least, are involved, or have been involved (in drug-trafficking)," prosecutor Jesse Rodriguez said in closing arguments on Friday.

One government witness, a now-jailed member of a drug cartel in northern Mexico, testified that the cartel paid bribes "all the way to the top in Mexico City," while another, a former Mexican police officer, said government planes were used to ferry drug bribes to officials in the Mexican capital.

A government win over Ruiz Massieu may be the harbinger of a new front for the U.S. war on drugs, namely the federal courts. A top U.S. drug agent told Reuters before the trial that "there will be a lot more of these kinds of trials coming up. You're going to see some interesting indictments this year."
